Coating of AFL and GDC via slot-die. Figure 6. AFL coatings with pump rate set to 50 RPM: (A) 3.5 FPM, (B) 3.7 FPM, (C) 4 FPM, (D) diluted, 3 FPM, and (E) diluted, 4 FPM. Figure 7. GDC coatings with pump rate set to 50 RPM: (A) 3 FPM, (B) 3.8 FPM, (C) 4 FPM, (D) 4.5 FPM and (E) 5 FPM. Figure 8. Dynamic viscosity curves indicating shear thinning behavior for all samples tested. The viscosity trend is GDC > AFL > ASL with higher solid content slurries, as expected, resulting in higher viscosity. Figure 9. Herschel–Bulkley model used in comparing shearing behavior in similar viscosity slurries. Figure 10. Amplitude sweep experiment showing data for the different solid loadings of the ASL, AFL and GDC slurries. Storage (closed symbol) and loss (open symbol) moduli. The LVR for each condition terminates at the marker on G’. Figure 11. Amplitude sweep experiment showing the tangent (G”/G’) of samples with varying solid loadings of the ASL, AFL and GDC slurries. A value above 1 can be considered to dominantly exhibit fluid behavior. Values below 1 indicate solid characteristics dominate, resulting in a rigid structure, which does not flow and can lead to permanent structural changes in response to stress. Figure 12. (Top) examples of non-Newtonian behavior from frequency sweep experiments. (Bottom) frequency sweep experiments of the ASL, AFL and GDC slurries at 70 wt%, 65 wt%, 60 wt% and 55 wt% solid content. The tangent is independent of the storage and loss moduli, indicating all three slurries exhibit gel behavior throughout the frequency range. Figure 13. Gelation value (J) of various slurries and solid contents. Figure 14. Doctor blade casting of the AFL slurry. Dried ASL coatings, followed by AFL, and GDC.
